gap: No result ChatGPT got states the cost per rated-lifetime kWh across the picks. Epoch's 48V 100Ah V2-T Elite costs $2,599 ÷ (5.12 kWh × 3,500 cycles) = $0.145 per kWh of rated throughput. That is about 2.4× EG4 LifePower4 V2 at $1,471 ÷ (5.12 × 0.80 × 6,000) = $0.060. The Pytes E-Box 48100R has the largest rated throughput, 27,648 kWh, but its continuous output is capped at 50 A, which is 2.56 kW.
standout_why: I checked three pages. liveoffthegrid.com/specs/batteries (cited) has $/kWh of nameplate only: EG4 V2 $287, Pytes V5 $283. It has no lifetime or per-cycle cost and no Wh/lb, and it does not list Epoch. Its EG4 V2 detail page gives only $0.048/kWh for EG4, which ignores the rated 80% DoD. ownyourelectricity.com gives no cycle counts and computes no lifetime cost. It also lists the Pytes E-Box 48100R at 5.1 kW continuous, but Pytes's own page says 50 A, about 2.56 kW. The EG4 V2 spec-sheet PDF ChatGPT cited would not extract as text, so I used EG4's product page. I couldn't load gearranking.com because of a certificate error, so I couldn't check it. No rival I could open puts EG4, Epoch and Pytes on one lifetime-cost basis.
decides: This backs EG4 LifePower4 V2 as best overall for solar. Per rated kWh delivered over its life it costs about 2.4× less than the Epoch 'premium' pick. Epoch's extra money buys self-heating, charging down to -22°F, an IP67 sealed case and an 11-year warranty, not more lifetime energy. Epoch also rates its 3,500 cycles to 70% remaining capacity and doesn't state the DoD. The Pytes E-Box has the most rated throughput, 6,000 cycles at 90% DoD, but it should be flagged: with 2.56 kW continuous per module, a 5 kW load needs two modules. Also note Epoch is $2,599 today on its own store, not the $2,399 ChatGPT showed.
